title: Salt going south, gold going north, and a caravan's survival riding on a courier sent ahead
register: documentary, resistant to the silent-trade legend
summary: No corporation, road, or ruler ever owned the whole of it: a chain of oasis wells, salt mines, river towns, and merchant diasporas moved rock salt south and gold north through many hands, taxed at every market it touched. Camels, Arabic contracts, and a courier sent ahead of the caravan with letters held it together across a desert that killed the careless. It did not end with Ghana's decline or Portugal's ships; it fractured when Morocco broke Songhay's power in 1591, and even then salt caravans, pilgrimage, and scholarship carried on.

nodes.name: Sijilmasa
nodes.note: Principal northern head of the western route: oasis, mint, and market from the ninth through fourteenth centuries. A hoard at Aqaba held 29 Sijilmasa dinars among 32 gold coins, proof of wide circulation though not of where each coin's metal was mined.

nodes.name: Tahert and Wargla
nodes.note: Ibadi merchant and religious centers supporting the earliest documented connections between North Africa and the western Sudan.

nodes.name: Tuwat and Gurara
nodes.note: A chain of oases increasingly important in the later medieval period, connecting the Niger bend and Taghaza to North Africa. Moroccan sixteenth-century policy took a direct interest in controlling its approaches.

nodes.name: Ghadames, Ghat and Zawila
nodes.note: Eastern Saharan nodes linking the Fezzan to the central Sudan, carrying captives, textiles, horses, and dates on a corridor less directly tied to Bambuk-Bure gold than Sijilmasa's western routes.

nodes.name: Awdaghost, Tegdaoust
nodes.note: Southern desert-edge market and intermediary between Sijilmasa and Ghana, at its peak in the ninth to eleventh centuries. Almoravid-associated forces took it in 1054-55; whether that event or a later one broke Ghana itself remains unresolved, and the two must not be conflated.

nodes.name: Tadmekka, Essouk
nodes.note: Early Islamic trading town between North Africa and Gao. Excavated molds interpreted as tools for processing very pure gold give rare material evidence of bullion-working at a Saharan entrepot rather than a merely literary report.

nodes.name: Taghaza
nodes.note: Salt-mining settlement and caravan junction. Ibn Battuta found buildings of salt slabs and camel hides here in 1352 and reports enslaved Massufa laborers cutting the salt. Contested between Songhay and Morocco, it was displaced by Moroccan pressure in the late sixteenth century.

nodes.name: Taoudenni
nodes.note: Replaced Taghaza as the dominant salt source feeding Timbuktu; the exact date and mechanism of the shift are not firmly established, but it belongs mainly to the post-medieval continuation of the trade.

nodes.name: Ijil
nodes.note: A major western Saharan salt source feeding routes toward Wadan and the Senegal valley, often overshadowed in narratives centered on Taghaza.

nodes.name: Bilma and Fachi
nodes.note: Salt and natron centers serving Agadez, the Hausa markets, and Lake Chad, forming a connected eastern branch of the caravan system.

nodes.name: Ghana, Koumbi Saleh
nodes.note: Royal center and market complex; al-Bakri describes two settlements six miles apart, one Muslim and scholarly, the other holding the king's palace and sacred grove. The identification of the site with Ghana's capital is widely used but not conclusively proven.

nodes.name: Takrur
nodes.note: An early Muslim-ruled polity and important western terminus; later writers sometimes generalized its name to a much larger region, complicating identification.

nodes.name: Walata, Iwalatan
nodes.note: Mali's northern reception point for caravans from Taghaza and Sijilmasa. Merchants there received advance letters and sent water parties into the desert to meet incoming travelers, at its peak in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

nodes.name: Timbuktu
nodes.note: Interface between camel traffic and Niger river transport, at its peak in the fourteenth through sixteenth centuries. Leo Africanus reported in the early sixteenth century that imported books yielded especially high profits, a sign that scholarship itself was cargo.

nodes.name: Gao and Gao-Saney
nodes.note: Royal and commercial center on the Niger linked to Tadmekka; excavations at Gao-Saney show imported glass and copper from the first millennium CE, securely demonstrating long-distance contact without proving every route it traveled.

nodes.name: Djenne and Djenne-jeno
nodes.note: Djenne-jeno's indigenous urban development began well before intensive Islamic trade, disproving the older claim that West African urbanism was wholly imported across the Sahara. The later Muslim town became a commercial and scholarly center connecting caravan termini to the delta.

nodes.name: Bambuk
nodes.region: between the Senegal and Falémé rivers
nodes.note: An auriferous region known to Arabic sources as a western producing zone. Exact mine locations, output, and political control are poorly documented; its identification is secure only at the regional level.

nodes.name: Bure
nodes.note: Upper Niger goldfield increasingly important to Mali, which could tax and influence routes and tribute without necessarily managing individual diggings.

nodes.name: Akan gold fields
nodes.note: Became increasingly important from the later medieval period; Portuguese coastal trade after the 1470s gave producers an additional outlet that supplemented rather than instantly displaced the northern routes.

nodes.name: Sao Jorge da Mina
nodes.note: Portuguese fort founded 1482 to draw Akan gold to the Atlantic coast, the clearest single marker of the coastal outlet competing with the Saharan routes.

nodes.name: Fez
nodes.note: Northern market and workshop city receiving Sijilmasa's traffic and, later, the Saadian state's claims on Sudanese revenue.

nodes.name: Cairo
nodes.note: Eastern terminus of the pilgrimage and scholarly routes. Mansa Musa's spending here in 1324-25 is credibly reported to have lowered gold's value relative to silver for a period, though exact totals cannot be treated as audited figures.

nodes.name: Wangara and Juula merchants
nodes.note: A collective designation in Arabic and African tradition for Mande-linked Muslim gold merchants and diasporas, not one centralized guild. Their multilingual capability, kinship networks, and Islamic literacy let them move between Muslim and non-Muslim political environments to aggregate gold toward savanna markets.

nodes.name: Sanhaja and Massufa
nodes.note: Saharan Berber-speaking groups supplying guides, camels, escorts, and messengers. Massufa laborers are the group Ibn Battuta explicitly names as enslaved at Taghaza's salt works in 1352.

nodes.name: North African merchant-financiers
nodes.note: Assembled investment capital under qiraḍ partnership contracts, bought cargo, hired agents, and converted gold into coin. A fatwa by al-Qabisi, who died in 1012, is direct evidence that Sudan-bound trade used such written investment contracts by the late tenth or early eleventh century.

nodes.name: Ghana rulers
nodes.note: Taxed trade, received tribute, and, according to al-Bakri, reserved large gold nuggets to themselves while letting dust circulate freely. His tax schedule, one dinar entering and two leaving per donkey-load of salt, is valuable but not independently audited.

nodes.name: Mali rulers
nodes.note: Integrated gold-producing approaches, Sahelian markets, and portions of desert traffic through tributary relations and negotiated allegiance rather than uniform territorial administration. Mansa Musa's 1324-25 pilgrimage made the empire legible to the wider Islamic world.

nodes.name: Songhay rulers
nodes.note: Sonni Ali and the Askia dynasty controlled the Niger bend, Timbuktu, Gao, and major traffic corridors until Judar Pasha's Moroccan expedition defeated Songhay forces at Tondibi in 1591.

nodes.name: Moroccan Saadian state
nodes.note: Under Ahmad al-Mansur claimed Taghaza as a taxable mine for the Muslim treasury and in 1590 dispatched Judar Pasha's expedition across the Sahara, breaking Songhay's imperial structure without ever achieving effortless control of the goldfields.

nodes.name: The takshif courier system
nodes.note: A hired Massufa courier carried a caravan's letters ahead to Walata so that friends or hosts could send a water party four nights into the desert to meet it. Its failure could leave merchants without a rendezvous, joining information directly to physical survival.

nodes.name: Mansa Musa
nodes.note: His 1324-25 hajj through Cairo was an exceptional royal expedition, not a normal caravan; al-Umari's account, compiled from interviews rather than eyewitness observation, remains the basis for most claims about its scale.

nodes.name: Ibn Battuta
nodes.note: Traveled from Sijilmasa through Taghaza and Walata to Mali in 1352-53, dictating the single best operational account of the route: travel times, water logistics, the takshif system, and salt prices rising from 8-10 mithqals at Walata to 20-30, sometimes 40, in Mali's capital.

nodes.name: Al-Bakri
nodes.note: Compiled the most detailed eleventh-century account of Ghana, Awdaghost, taxes, and trade, drawing on earlier merchants' and geographers' reports though he never visited West Africa himself.

nodes.name: Enslaved captives in transit
nodes.note: Captives were exported north, worked salt deposits and domestic establishments, and were traded as women and children as well as men. Ibn Battuta traveled north with a convoy including about 600 enslaved women, a report about one caravan, not an annual total; no defensible aggregate figure exists for the medieval period.

nodes.name: Camel caravans
nodes.note: Dromedary trains carrying salt, cloth, dates, and copper south and gold, ivory, and captives north across waterless stages measured in days rather than surveyed distances; camel breed, load, and season made any single fixed load figure false precision.

nodes.name: Niger river canoe traffic
nodes.note: Canoes moved bulky salt and grain more cheaply than overland transport, linking Timbuktu, Gao, and Djenne with smaller settlements; Ibn Battuta himself traveled part of his route by water.

edges.note: The classic ninth-eleventh-century western corridor; al-Bakri's itinerary suggests roughly two months between major termini, but no universal schedule existed.
Ibn Battuta's caravan took about 25 days over this stage in 1352.
A ten-night waterless crossing followed by a rest at Tasarahla and the dispatch of the takshif courier ahead.
Central corridor connecting Saharan merchants to the Niger bend, secured by archaeological imports and gold-processing remains at Tadmekka.
Salt carried south for redistribution; grain moved north because the mining settlement could not feed itself.
Taoudenni's successor route once it replaced Taghaza as the dominant salt source.
The eastern branch, later called taghlamt in regional usage.
Niger river traffic linking the two Songhay commercial centers.
Redistribution toward the Inland Niger Delta and southern production zones.
Gold aggregated from the producing zone toward the royal market and its taxation.
Grew more important to Mali as Ghana's older Bambuk-facing routes declined.
The Atlantic outlet that supplemented, rather than immediately replaced, the northern Saharan routes after 1482.
The pilgrimage and scholarly route; carried gold, letters, and gifts eastward and books, teachers, and legal ideas back.
The 1324-25 hajj; al-Umari records that Musa's spending affected the value of gold relative to silver in the city for a period.
Departed at the beginning of Muharram 753 AH, February 1352, with the caravan of Abu Muhammad Yandakan al-Massufi.
Al-Bakri compiled his account in al-Andalus from earlier reports and never visited Ghana himself; the tax schedule he preserves is valuable but not independently audited.
A letter carried ahead so that a water party could meet the caravan four nights out.
Massufa laborers worked the salt; Ibn Battuta names this group explicitly as enslaved.
Qirad partnerships financed Sudan-bound ventures; al-Qabisi's fatwa, before his death in 1012, shows jurists already weighing the enforceability of such contracts across jurisdictions.
One dinar on an incoming donkey-load of salt, two on an outgoing load, by al-Bakri's account.
Contested between Songhay and Morocco over taxation of the mine before the 1591 conquest.
A surviving diplomatic letter claims the mine's revenue for the Muslim treasury and proposes a tax of one mithqal per camel, a political claim rather than proof of uncontested possession.
Judar Pasha's expedition defeated Songhay forces at Tondibi in 1591, a date given as 12 April by Taʾrikh al-Sudan and as March by other Moroccan, Spanish, and Sudanese sources.
The northbound trade in captives; Ibn Battuta's own return caravan included a trader with roughly 600 enslaved women, a single convoy's figure, not an annual volume.
